findings.antecedent: positive appraisal of grass environment (affordances for walking/playing)
findings.quote: The positive appraisal of that environment would thus have generated a corresponding post-cognitive effect and elicited post-cognitive arousal ('Arousal3'; Ulrich, 1983). Higher PA in turn reduces the urge to mobilise the cognitive re-sources that are necessary to counter a threat (Russell & Mehrabian, 1978). This would explain why the SCLs of participants in the grass group con-tinued to decline even in the final minutes of VR immersion.

limitations: Controlled leaves/blades of grass did not sway as in real life, potentially affecting results.
Compared only two types of vegetation; future research should examine a greater variety of vegetation types with different textures and forms.
Compared vegetation in a single courtyard setting; future research should explore effects of vegetation in other settings (e.g., open fields).
Observed SCL responses for only 9 min of VR immersion; SCL trends in grass/tree groups showed different trends in the final minute, suggesting longer immersion periods are needed.
Study conducted with virtual environments instead of real ones, requiring caution in generalizing results to real landscape designs without additional in situ testing.
Did not test immersion effect or VR quality in the experiment.
Single study; additional studies with VR or real environments are needed for generalizable findings.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the restorative effects of different urban virtual reality (VR) environments (concrete, grass, or trees) on stress reduction. Participants were first stressed with a math test and noise, then immersed in one of the VR environments for 10 minutes while skin conductance levels (SCLs) and affect were measured. Key findings indicate that both grass and tree environments significantly reduced SCLs compared to concrete-only environments during the latter half of immersion, and the grass environment had the strongest positive effect on positive affect. Negative affect decreased across all environments but showed no significant differences between them. Limitations include the use of static VR environments, limited vegetation types and settings, and a relatively short immersion period, suggesting caution in generalizing results to real-world landscape design.
